title: Fort Lupton Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Fort Lupton wells have a 49-foot median depth, but some reach 1,166 feet. See yields, water levels, permits, and drilling costs.
intro_html:
Fort Lupton sits on the plains, where well records show a wide range of conditions. Among permitted wells within 5 miles, the median reported depth is 49 feet, but the middle half runs from 30 to 378 feet. That spread matters when you are pricing a lot, because a shallow well is common in the records while some sites require much deeper drilling.

Reported production is generally workable: the median yield is 13.0 gallons per minute. Still, only part of the permit record includes yield or water-level information. A site-specific review of nearby wells, the intended use, septic layout, and the applicable DWR permit rules should come before you buy or build.

sections.heading: Fort Lupton well depths vary sharply by site
sections.html:
Fort Lupton’s depth numbers are pulled in two directions. Sixty-six percent of wells are under 100 feet, while 20% are at least 600 feet. The deepest recorded well is 1,166 feet. The median of 49 feet is useful for orientation, but it is not a bid for a particular parcel.

The aquifer names on permits help explain the variation. Records include 2,661 unnamed or fractured-bedrock wells, 750 Laramie Fox Hills wells, and 478 alluvial wells. All recorded aquifer wells are Denver Basin aquifer wells. In Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock, a driller should use nearby construction records to set a realistic depth allowance instead of relying only on the local median.

sections.heading: What Fort Lupton wells produce
sections.html:
Among wells reporting a pump yield, the median is 13.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 10.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. The records show 44% producing more than 15 gallons per minute, and another 51% between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. Only 5% are in the 1-to-5 gallon-per-minute range, and none are reported below 1 gallon per minute.

That is encouraging for ordinary household demand, but yield is not the same as storage or guaranteed long-term supply. Ask for a pump test and review the well construction before assuming the result will support irrigation, livestock, or additional connections. Household-use wells are commonly subject to exempt-well rules, including the 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit.

sections.heading: Water levels near Fort Lupton need careful reading
sections.html:
The median reported static water level is 20 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 10 to 258 feet. That is a broad range. A shallow water level can simplify pumping, but it does not by itself prove that a well has good quality or adequate production.

The decade series does not show a simple steadily dropping table. Median depth to water was 17 feet in the 1960s, 358 feet in the 1990s, 94 feet in the 2000s, 45 feet in the 2010s, and 12 feet in the 2020s. Measurement locations and well types differ, so treat the series as context, not a parcel-specific forecast.

sections.heading: Permit history and drillers around Fort Lupton
sections.html:
Permit activity is strongest in the more recent record. The data show 100 permits in the 1950s, 202 in the 1960s, 360 in the 1970s, 290 in the 1980s, 702 in the 1990s, 1,082 in the 2000s, 732 in the 2010s, and 455 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2026.

The most active names in these records are Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 884 wells, Glover’s Drilling, with 241, and Roger Schocke Well Drlg. Inc., with 186. Those counts describe permit records, not current availability or a recommendation. Confirm licensing, insurance, scheduling, and the exact scope of a written bid before hiring.

sections.heading: Fort Lupton well drilling cost range
sections.html:
For the local cost model, drilling in Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock is estimated at $50 to $70 per foot. Applied to the 49-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $2,400 to $3,400. That is only the hole, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $8,400 to $15,400 at the median depth. A deeper site can move well beyond that range because depth affects drilling, casing, pump selection, and electrical work. Get the bid separated into drilling, casing and grout, development, pump equipment, trenching, and testing so you can compare proposals on the same basis.

sections.heading: Risks to check before buying near Fort Lupton
sections.html:
The record contains many productive wells, but buyers still need to verify the individual parcel. Only 2,951 wells report a total depth, 980 report a pump yield, and 287 report a static water level. Missing data means a nearby map point may not answer the questions that matter for your property.

Environmental screening also deserves attention. Within about 10 miles are 1,481 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 14 historic mine features, and 5 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These mapped sites do not prove contamination at your lot. Order a water-quality test, inspect the wellhead and casing, and keep septic setbacks, replacement area, driveway access, and building placement in the design. In an over-appropriated basin, confirm whether an augmentation plan or other approval is required.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a Fort Lupton lot
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, not the Fort Lupton median. Pull DWR permits for the property and compare construction depth, aquifer, yield, static level, and use with nearby wells in Aristocrat Ranchettes, Lochbuie, Brighton, Todd Creek, Dacono, and Frederick. Nearby records can reveal whether the lot resembles the shallow majority or the much deeper part of the local range.

Before closing, make the contract contingent on a well inspection, water-quality testing, and confirmation that the intended household, stock, or irrigation use is permitted. If you are building, have the driller, septic designer, and excavator coordinate the well location, tank, electrical route, access drive, and septic replacement area. A well that produces water still has to fit the site and the permit.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Fort Lupton?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Fort Lupton is 49 feet. The middle half runs from 30 to 378 feet, while the deepest recorded well is 1,166 feet. Depth varies substantially by parcel and aquifer. Nearby permits are more useful for estimating a new well than the median alone.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Fort Lupton?
faq.a: The local model uses $50 to $70 per foot. At the 49-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $2,400 to $3,400. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is about $8,400 to $15,400. Deeper drilling or difficult access can increase the project cost.

faq.q: Do Fort Lupton wells produce enough water for a home?
faq.a: Reported yields are generally favorable. The median is 13.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half is 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. The records show 44% above 15 gallons per minute and 5% between 1 and 5. Confirm the individual well’s pump test, storage, and permitted use before relying on it.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Fort Lupton?
faq.a: Permit records do not establish that water is safe to drink. About 10 miles of the area includes 1,481 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, plus 5 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those locations do not prove contamination on your parcel, but buyers should test the well water and inspect construction before closing.

faq.q: Are Fort Lupton water levels going down?
faq.a: The available decade medians do not show a simple steady decline. Reported depth to water was 17 feet in the 1960s, 358 feet in the 1990s, 94 feet in the 2000s, 45 feet in the 2010s, and 12 feet in the 2020s. Because wells and measurement locations differ, use the figures as context rather than a parcel-specific trend.
